neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Affect is anxious but cooperative. Speech is fluent with normal rate, rhythm, and prosody. No dysarthria. Attention intact, able to recite months of the year backward. Memory 3/3 immediate and delayed recall. No aphasia. Fund of knowledge intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Fundoscopic exam normal, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or diplopia. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation, no facial droop. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in all extremities, no spasticity or rigidity. Right lower extremity: give-way weakness pattern noted in hip flexion, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion — initial resistance to full strength followed by sudden collapse of effort. Formal testing yields 2-3/5 in these muscle groups with inconsistency on repeat testing. Left lower extremity: 5/5 throughout. Upper extremities: 5/5 bilaterally. Hoover sign POSITIVE on the right — involuntary hip extension on the right is strong when testing left hip flexion against resistance, but voluntary right hip flexion appears weak. No pronator drift in upper extremities.
neurological_exam.sensory: Patient reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the entire right leg extending to the level of the inguinal crease, with a sharp midline demarcation that splits the trunk exactly at the midline. Vibration and proprioception are reported as diminished in the right toes, but testing with distraction shows intact proprioception. Left leg sensation intact throughout. Upper extremity sensation intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally (including right side despite reported weakness), Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally. Heel-to-shin testing normal on the left; patient reports inability to perform on the right due to weakness, but when distracted the right leg moves smoothly to the shin. No intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact in upper extremities.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient walks with a dragging right leg pattern. The gait is effortful-appearing but non-physiological — the leg drags behind with the hip externally rotated but knee does not buckle. When distracted during conversation while ambulating, leg function intermittently improves. No circumduction. Romberg testing: marked swaying with eyes closed but catches herself repeatedly without falling (positive for functional sway). Tandem gait not attempted by patient due to reported weakness.
neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a paroxysmal episode of bilateral upper extremity shaking lasting approximately 90 seconds. Eyes were tightly closed with resistance to opening, and she appeared to retain awareness (responded to verbal commands during the event). The shaking was irregular, variable in amplitude, and waxed and waned. No tonic phase, no cyanosis, no tongue biting, no urinary incontinence. She was immediately alert and conversant after the episode with no post-ictal confusion.

patient.chief_complaint: Right leg weakness and episodes of shaking spells over the past 3 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Crystal Morris is a 34-year-old right-handed woman and elementary school teacher who presents as an inpatient transfer from the emergency department after three weeks of progressive right leg weakness and recurrent episodes of uncontrollable shaking. The symptoms began abruptly three weeks ago when she awoke one morning and found that her right leg felt heavy and difficult to move. She reports that she was unable to bear weight on the right leg and fell twice that first day. Over the following days, the weakness persisted and she began using a cane provided by a friend. Approximately one week after the onset of weakness, she experienced her first shaking episode while at home: her arms and legs began trembling, she fell to the floor, and the episode lasted roughly two minutes. Her boyfriend witnessed the event and reports that she appeared awake during the episode and could respond to her name, though she later described feeling detached from her body. She has since had five additional similar episodes, occurring roughly every two to three days, sometimes triggered by emotional stress or arguments. Emergency medical services were called during the third episode and she was brought to the emergency department, where a CT head was normal and she was discharged with neurology follow-up. She returned to the ED two days ago after two episodes occurred in the same day, one at home and one in the waiting room of her primary care physician's office. The waiting room episode was witnessed by nursing staff, who noted bilateral arm shaking with eyes closed and no loss of continence. She was admitted for further workup. She denies headache, visual changes, numbness or tingling in the upper extremities, bowel or bladder incontinence, fever, weight loss, or recent illness. She reports significant emotional distress related to work stress, relationship difficulties, and learning of a close friend's cancer diagnosis shortly before symptom onset. She was previously seen by a psychiatrist for anxiety and depression but has not had regular follow-up in the past year.

output.summary: Functional neurological disorder is characterized by positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency. CBT adapted for functional neurological symptoms shows efficacy in reducing non-epileptic attack frequency (CODES RCT evidence). Specialized physiotherapy using motor retraining techniques demonstrates benefit for functional motor symptoms in observational and controlled studies. Psychiatric comorbidities including anxiety, depression, and PTSD are present in the majority of published cohorts. Anti-seizure medications have not demonstrated efficacy for non-epileptic attacks in controlled trials.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with motor symptoms (right leg weakness) and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Sudden focal deficit raises stroke; non-anatomical weakness pattern with positive Hoover sign, normal MRI/DWI, and intact reflexes argue against vascular etiology.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

useless_tools.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

Nerve conduction studies and EMG have no role once positive functional signs are documented: the deficit is not neuromuscular, the study is uncomfortable, and a normal result reinforces the patient's search for an organic cause — the principal iatrogenic harm in this condition
Somatosensory evoked potentials answer a question about a lesion in the somatosensory pathway; a midline-splitting, non-anatomical sensory deficit is not that question

critical_actions: Do NOT make the diagnosis by exclusion: document at least one positive rule-in sign, which is the act that establishes it
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
Do not give gadolinium without a specific indication — contrast adds cost and risk and answers no question that positive functional signs have not already answered

Do not repeat the brain MRI, the laboratory panel or the lumbar puncture once a first normal study and positive rule-in signs are documented: each repetition strengthens the patient's belief that something organic has been missed
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).

Brain MRI and basic laboratory testing are OPTIONAL here, not due diligence: the diagnosis rests on the positive signs, and each additional negative study is a cost and an iatrogenic harm rather than a confirmation. Where imaging is recommended in this case it is for one specific alternative question, once.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of multiple sclerosis in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a demyelinating diagnosis (MS) and pursue extensive MS-specific workup before considering FND
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-first-degree family history of MS is a weak risk factor; the patient's symptoms must be evaluated on positive findings. Normal brain MRI without demyelinating lesions effectively addresses this concern.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of epilepsy in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of epilepsy does not establish the patient's events as epileptic. Video-EEG capturing the habitual event without ictal correlate is the gold standard.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety or depression) in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Symptom onset coincident with a major psychosocial stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.

clinical_pearls: Hoover sign is the most validated positive clinical sign for functional leg weakness and can be demonstrated at bedside
Eyes closed during a seizure-like event strongly suggests PNES — epileptic seizures typically present with eyes open
FND is one of the most common reasons for neurological outpatient referrals, affecting up to 16% of neurology clinic patients
A family history of epilepsy does not increase the patient's own risk of FND being epilepsy — each case must be evaluated independently with EEG
